prompt.context: Our client is a large car manufacturer that has been facing financial stress for the past few years. To overcome this crisis, they bought a small bank and started offering a lease at a lower rate than other car manufacturers. This move has positioned the client strategically in the market and has helped them regain market share. However, customers are now complaining of poor customer service in the banking division. The client has reached out to help them improve their banking division customer service. In particular, they want to create a call center to provide support to all lease customers, but they do not know how big this call center should be.
prompt.question: How many employees do they need to hire for this call center?

clarifying_info.q: Does the bank offer leases for other manufacturers' cars as well?
clarifying_info.a: No. The bank offers the lease only for cars from its parent company.

clarifying_info.q: Does the call center also handle prospective customers or only existing lease holders?
clarifying_info.a: The call center is focused only on clients that have already signed the lease contract. It does not attend to prospective customers.

clarifying_info.q: What is the population of the US?
What age range buys new cars?
What is the life expectancy and is the population uniformly distributed?
clarifying_info.a: Life expectancy is 80 years and the population is uniformly distributed among all ages.

clarifying_info.q: What share of people are willing to buy a new car given the current crisis?
clarifying_info.a: With the current crisis, only 50% of the population is willing to buy new cars; the rest prefer used cars.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average lifetime of a car?
What is the client's market share?
What percentage of the client's customers use the lease?
clarifying_info.a: 40% of the client's customers use the lease to acquire the car.

clarifying_info.q: How often do customers call the call center?
clarifying_info.a: Customers call only once a year until the end of the lease contract.

clarifying_info.q: Are calls uniformly distributed throughout the day and year?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume all calls are uniformly distributed throughout the year and during the day with no peak periods.

clarifying_info.q: What are the employee work hours?
clarifying_info.a: Union contract states employees can only work 6 hours per day, 6 days per week.

clarifying_info.q: What hours is the call center open?
clarifying_info.a: The call center receives calls only from 8am to 8pm, Monday to Sunday (12 hours per day, 7 days per week).

clarifying_info.q: How long is the average call?
How many days are in a year for this analysis?

framework: Estimate total number of cars sold in the US per year using population-based market sizing
Apply client market share to get annual cars sold by the client
Apply lease take-up rate to get annual new lease customers
Apply lease length to convert annual new customers into the total active customer base making calls per year
Convert total annual calls into daily call demand (in minutes)
Determine how many employee-hours the call center operates each day (12-hour window, 7 days)
Calculate employees needed per day to cover demand, then adjust for the 6-day work week constraint

questions.prompt: How many cars are sold in the US each year?
questions.guidance: Candidate should derive the number of potential car buyers from population, filter by age range (20-60 = 50% of 80-year lifespan), apply the 50% new-car preference, then divide by car lifetime to get annual purchases.

math.setup: Eligible buyers = Population x (age range / life expectancy) x new-car share; Annual sales = Eligible buyers / car lifetime
steps: Eligible buyers = 300M x (40/80) x 50% = 300M x 50% x 50% = 75M
Annual US car sales = 75M / 5 = 15M cars per year
math.answer: 15 million cars sold per year in the US

questions.prompt: How many of the client's customers sign a lease each year?
questions.guidance: Apply client market share then lease take-up rate sequentially.

math.setup: Client annual sales = US sales x market share; Lease customers = Client sales x lease rate
steps: Client annual sales = 15M x 10% = 1.5M cars per year
Lease customers per year = 1.5M x 40% = 0.6M customers per year
math.answer: 0.6 million (600,000) new lease customers per year

questions.prompt: How many total calls must the call center handle per year, and how does that translate to daily call demand in minutes?
questions.guidance: Multiply annual new customers by lease length to get total calls per year (each customer calls once per year for 3 years). Then divide by 360 to get daily calls and multiply by call duration.

math.setup: Total calls/year = new customers/year x lease length; Calls/day = total calls / 360; Daily demand (min) = calls/day x avg call length
steps: Total calls per year = 0.6M x 3 = 1.8M calls
Daily demand in minutes = 5,000 x 5 min = 25,000 minutes
math.answer: 25,000 minutes of call demand per day

questions.prompt: How many employees must be scheduled each day to cover the call volume, and how many must be hired accounting for days off?
questions.guidance: The call center is open 12 hours (720 minutes) per day. Each employee works 6 hours (360 minutes) per day. Divide total daily demand by minutes available per employee per day to get employees needed on any given day. Then adjust upward because employees work only 6 of 7 days while the call center is open all 7 days.

math.setup: Employees on shift = daily demand (min) / minutes per employee per day; Hiring adjustment for 6-day week = on-shift employees x (7/6), i.e. add 1/6 as buffer
steps: Minutes available per employee per day = 6 hours x 60 min = 360 min
Call center open 7 days, employees work 6 days: adjustment factor = 7/6
Total hires needed = 70 x 7/6 = 70 + 70 x (1/6) ≈ 70 + 11.7 ≈ 82 employees
math.answer: Approximately 82 employees need to be hired

questions.prompt: The client does not have enough budget to hire all 82 employees. What would you suggest to reduce the number of employees needed?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that employees needed = f(call volume, call duration). Reducing either lever shrinks headcount. Strong answers cover both levers with specific, practical ideas.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific ideas would you suggest to reduce the number of call center employees needed?

categories.name: Reduce number of calls
ideas: Develop a customer-facing website that easily provides lease information self-service
Map the most common questions and publish a FAQ on the customer website
Offer an alternative communication channel such as live chat to deflect phone volume

categories.name: Reduce average call length
ideas: Invest in voice recognition technology to faster identify the customer's problem before routing to an operator
Provide targeted employee training to resolve issues more quickly
Build a pre-call authentication flow so agents do not spend time verifying identity on the call

recommendation: The client needs to hire approximately 82 employees to staff the call center, based on 1.8 million calls per year at 5 minutes per call across a 12-hour, 7-day operation with employees limited to 6 hours per day and 6 days per week
Given budget constraints, the client should pursue simultaneous demand-reduction initiatives — particularly a self-service website with FAQ — to reduce call volume before finalizing headcount
risks: Call volume could be higher if customers call more than once per year or if onboarding issues spike early in the lease
Union constraints or turnover could increase effective headcount needs beyond 82
next_steps: Quantify self-service deflection potential to resize headcount target
Pilot the call center at smaller scale and measure actual call frequency and duration before full hiring
Evaluate phased hiring tied to lease portfolio growth
